citing_sentences: However, existing paradigms [40, 9, 19, 56, 33, 45] typically accommodate interactive controls through separate modules (e.g., AdaLN modulation), which tends to isolate different control signals and leaves their cross-dependencies to be captured only indirectly, as shown in Figure 2 (Left).

To avoid the scalability bottleneck of fragmented side channels (e.g., AdaLN or separate cross-attention layers), World-in-Context casts diverse interactive signals directly into sequence tokens within a unified attention space, as shown in Figure 2 (Right).

citing_sentences: To validate the efficacy of explicit view conditioning, we compare our formulation against a baseline that specifies view modes through text alone (“w/o view modeling") Figure 4 evaluates trajectory oscillations under Fpp and Free conditioning across $100$ scenes, while Figure 3 presents qualitative transitions alongside quantitative evaluations on the WBench Fpp$\leftrightarrow$Tpp suite.

Because view tokens act as modular contextual switches within the shared attention space, training exclusively on single-view clips already gives rise to perspective transitions simply by varying the view token sequence during rollout, as shown in Figure 3.

As shown in Figure 4, text-based conditioning yields closely overlapping oscillation profiles for Fpp and Free, conflating their respective physical semantics.

abstract: Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion. Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly. In this work, we present World-in-Context, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC). Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways, World-in-Context unifies view, action, and camera controls into explicit tokens contextualized directly within a shared self-attention space. Our formulation reveals that (i) explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting dynamics and unlock emergent view switching from single-view data, while (ii) action and camera inputs play complementary roles in governing local responsiveness and global stability. To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions. On WBench, World-in-Context-5B achieves navigation performance on par with 22B EchoWM ($81.5$ vs. $81.6$) and attains a $93.8\%$ perspective-switching success rate, substantially outperforming existing 5B baselines ($18.8\%$). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages of World-in-Context under richer conditioning mixtures, favorable data efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts.

sections.body: The paper argues that current interactive pipelines leave view mode implicit in text captions and treat camera trajectories as the main control, which blurs action and camera motion. It proposes World-in-Context, which encodes view, action and camera controls as tokens in a shared self-attention space, and IT-RoPE, a positional encoding that adds control transitions to temporal attention. The stated evidence is WBench results: World-in-Context-5B reaches 81.5 navigation against 81.6 for the 22B EchoWM, and 93.8% perspective-switching success against 18.8% for existing 5B baselines.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Interactive world models need explicit view modes and separate action and camera controls, which current pipelines leave implicit or conflated.

sections.body: This section places the work among interactive video world models and in-context conditioning. It states that prior models mostly use continuous camera trajectories, often treat view perspective implicitly in text, and in some cases route actions and camera poses through separate architectural pathways. The authors say they instead keep view modes explicit and treat character actions and camera motion as coexisting, independent controls in one attention space. For in-context conditioning, it summarizes prior work on shared attention contexts for image and video generation and notes that IC-World applies it to consistency across observations of one world. The section gives no experiments.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior interactive models leave view implicit and rely mostly on camera trajectories, and this work extends in-context conditioning to them.

sections.body: This section defines the task as generating future video from a context specification and per-frame user inputs. It describes existing models as injecting controls through condition-specific modules, such as modulation for camera trajectories, additive token injection for discrete actions, and cross-attention for text controls. The authors argue these separate parameter spaces hinder capturing cross-condition dependencies. Instead, they cast the controls as condition tokens concatenated with the visual latents and processed by one flow-matching backbone. The section gives the formulation only and reports no results.
sections.heading: Preliminary: Problem Formulation
sections.headline: Existing models inject controls through condition-specific pathways, while the paper recasts them as condition tokens concatenated with visual latents.

sections.body: This section defines the unified condition sequence of view, action and camera tokens, and IT-RoPE, a positional encoding that adds accumulated control transitions to temporal attention. View modes are learned categorical tokens for Free, first-person and third-person regimes. Compared with a text-only view baseline across 100 scenes, explicit view modeling yields distinct oscillation profiles for first-person and Free motion, where text conditioning overlaps them. Trained only on single-view clips, the base model reaches a 37.5% view-switching success rate, against 6.25% for the text baseline. Adding 500 transition sequences raises it to 93.8%. Switches without fine-tuning show residual artifacts. Action tokens separate discrete key states from continuous motion, and camera tokens use Plücker ray encodings.
sections.heading: World-in-Context
sections.headline: Explicit view tokens separate free-camera and first-person motion, and view switching emerges from single-view training.

sections.body: This section compares World-in-Context with 5B baselines that share the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbone and with larger models. On WBench Navigation it reports an average of 81.5, close to Zing-0.5 at 81.0 and EchoWM at 81.6, with Interaction raised from 84.2 to 86.0. Ablations report that the in-context advantage grows with richer controls, reaching 81.2 navigation and 86.8 interaction, and that IT-RoPE raises navigation from 80.5 to 81.2. ICC reaches 75.0% switching with 50K+250 clips. Training-data scales of other methods are not consistently disclosed.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: World-in-Context-5B nearly matches the 22B EchoWM on navigation and reaches 93.8% perspective-switching success, versus 18.8% for the best 5B baseline.

sections.body: This section extends the method to streaming causal rollouts, where historical latents are added to the shared attention sequence through sink and recent-window tokens instead of a KV cache. WiC-Causal reaches 81.2 average navigation and 90.6% perspective-switching success on WBench, against 81.5 and 93.8% for the bidirectional model, and it still exceeds the 5B baselines. The qualitative rollouts show long-horizon coherence and reproduced landmarks in loop closures. A second extension, WiC-Game, adds fire, duck and walk tokens trained on a single Counter-Strike 2 map, and is evaluated qualitatively on unseen maps and real-world starting images. No quantitative game results are reported.
sections.heading: Applicability of World-in-Context
sections.headline: A causal variant reaches 81.2 navigation and 90.6% perspective-switching success, and the method also extends to game controls.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that World-in-Context unifies view mode, character action and camera trajectory as tokens in a shared attention space. It reports 81.5 navigation on WBench, on par with the 22B EchoWM, and 93.8% perspective-switching success, and it restates the findings on compounding gains under richer conditioning, sample efficiency and causal rollouts. The positioning paragraph says the work centers on algorithmic formulation rather than a full system, and that overall capacity depends on data quality, model size and training scale. The training set is a modest 100K navigation clips with 500 switching sequences. Cross-method data-scale comparisons are omitted from the main table because training statistics are not consistently disclosed.
sections.heading: Conclusion and Positioning
sections.headline: The paper states its training set is modest and that its focus is algorithmic formulation rather than a full system or scaling study.

sections.body: The appendix describes the training mixture of 100K navigation clips from datasets such as DL3DV, RealEstate and Sekai, plus 500 switching sequences from EgoExo and internal data. It lists a three-stage filtering pipeline covering shot continuity, motion and aesthetics. Control annotation uses a vision-language model for view mode, ViPE-reconstructed camera trajectories, and actions inverted from those trajectories. Table 3 gives navigation source shares, with DL3DV at 29.22%. It also gives the two-stage curriculum with an 8K mix, the mixed action-camera conditioning schedule, IT-RoPE implementation details, and the WBench evaluation and analysis setups.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists data sources, quality filters, control annotation, two-stage training schedule, positional-encoding details and evaluation protocols.
